paras: The police killing of Frank Hagan took place near Leavenworth, Kansas, in early August 1882, when a policeman shot Hagan, a Black man, three times while trying to arrest him after a shooting at an emancipation celebration. Hagan died on August 4, and a coroner's inquest exculpated the officer, identified in a follow-up dispatch as Policeman Shepherd. The story ran as a short telegraphic item in papers from Memphis to Savannah, one of which headed it "A Negro Desperado Killed."

The trouble began at an emancipation celebration held by "a party of colored people" at Reiger's Grove, outside Leavenworth. According to the wire, Hagan and a man named Tom Sanders "got into a row," and a later dispatch said the quarrel had started "over a chew of tobacco."

When Bob Jackson stepped in "to preserve peace," Hagan was said to have shot him in the arm, and King Robinson, described as an ex-policeman, was also shot. Hagan then took refuge in the house of a white woman nearby. By the dispatch's account, when a policeman entered to arrest him Hagan struck him with a chair, and the officer shot him three times, "the third ball passing through his body." This version of the shooting comes from the police side, and no other witness is quoted.

Hagan died at 2:30 on the morning of August 4. An inquest the same day "excupated" Policeman Shepherd, and no report of any further charge or proceeding against the officer appears in the coverage. Nor does the coverage say what became of Jackson, Robinson or Sanders.

The first account was a Leavenworth dispatch dated August 2, which the Memphis Public Ledger printed that day and the two Wheeling papers on August 3. A shorter version, saying only that Hagan "shot and wounded two men" and "resisted arrest," appeared in Wheeling, Richmond, Savannah and Knoxville papers between August 3 and 4. Headlines ranged from "Celebrating Their Freedom" and "Fatal Affray in Kansas" to the Savannah Morning News's "A Negro Desperado Killed."

Every version presented the police account as fact, and the Wheeling Register ran the inquest news under the heading "Murder Over a Chew of Tobacco." The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian reprinted the item on August 8 in a column of brief notes, naming King Robinson as the policeman who killed him. No Kansas paper's report was found, and the Black press of 1882 lies outside the searched collection.

The detailed dispatch placed the shooting on the afternoon of August 2, while the shorter version, under the same dateline, said "yesterday," implying August 1. The officer is unnamed in the first dispatches, called Shepherd in the August 4 report and Robinson in the South Kentuckian; because the fuller wire describes Robinson as a wounded ex-policeman, the Shepherd attribution, tied to the inquest, is the better attested. The victim's surname was printed as Hagan, Hagen, Hogen and Hogan, and the man shot in the arm as Bob Jackson or Bob Johnson.

bases: A policeman attempting an arrest shot Hagan three times in a house near the celebration grounds, and no crowd took part in the killing (A10, A11, A18).

accounts.label: Detailed wire (Leavenworth, Aug. 2)
accounts.gist: Hagan shot a peacemaker in the arm during a row, Robinson was also shot, and Hagan hid in a white woman's house; when a policeman entered he struck him with a chair and was shot three times.

accounts.label: Short wire (Leavenworth, Aug. 2)
accounts.gist: Hagan 'shot and wounded two men' the day before and, resisting arrest, was mortally wounded by a policeman.

accounts.label: Follow-up dispatch (Leavenworth, Aug. 4)
accounts.gist: Hagan, shot by Policeman Shepherd, died early Aug. 4; an inquest exculpated Shepherd; the quarrel reportedly began over a chew of tobacco.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the short wire under neutral heads such as 'Celebrating Their Freedom' and 'Fatal Affray in Kansas', presenting the police account as fact.
The Savannah Morning News headed the wire 'A Negro Desperado Killed'.
The Wheeling Register headed the follow-up 'Murder Over a Chew of Tobacco', locating the cause in the quarrel rather than the police shooting.

conflicts.note: Both versions carry an Aug. 2 dateline; the Public Ledger printed the 'this afternoon' version on Aug. 2 itself, which fits a same-day event, but neither is a local account.

versions.value: Unnamed policeman; King Robinson an ex-policeman who was himself shot

conflicts.note: The Aug. 4 dispatch ties Shepherd to an inquest and the fuller wire makes Robinson a wounded bystander, so the South Kentuckian brief appears to have conflated roles.

record_check.dossier: One man, Frank Hagan, also printed Hagen, Hogen and Hogan.
Shot Aug. 2 per the detailed wire or Aug. 1 per the short wire; died Aug. 4.
Policeman Shepherd (A18); the South Kentuckian names King Robinson (A19).
Hagan is accused of wounding two men, Bob Jackson and King Robinson, at a celebration 'by a party of colored people'; neither man's race is stated, and they were injured by Hagan, not by the police.
Shot while a policeman was trying to arrest him.
The police shooting took place in a white woman's house near the grove; an inquest exculpated Policeman Shepherd and Hagan died Aug. 4.
First printed Aug. 2 (Memphis Public Ledger); at least eight papers.

info: Shot August 2, 1882, 'this afternoon' per the detailed wire; 'yesterday' (August 1) per the short wire, both datelined August 2; died about 2:30 a.m. August 4.
Quarrel at an emancipation celebration at Reiger's (Rieger's) Grove near Leavenworth; police shooting in the nearby house of a white woman.
Frank Hagan, also printed Hagen, Hogen, Hogan; described as 'the negro' and 'the colored man'.
Accused of shooting Bob Jackson (or Johnson) in the arm during a row with Tom Sanders; King Robinson, an ex-policeman, was also shot; accused of striking the arresting policeman with a chair.
An unnamed policeman in the first wire; 'Policeman Shepherd' in the Aug. 4 dispatch; 'policeman King Robinson' in the South Kentuckian.
Hagan died of his wound; no arrest, charge or trial of the officer was reported.
